# Who really recycles the Philippines' electronic trash? Ask the informal waste pickers.

In Malabon, informal waste pickers like Joanna Amican dismantle electronics with bare hands to survive, breathing in toxic metal dust and fibers. Now they're organizing to demand legal recognition and protection.

By Alex Lauricio · 7 min read · Updated September 15, 2026 · Metro Manila

waste management

Image: Who really recycles the Philippines' electronic trash? Ask the informal waste pickers.

CITY OF MALABON, Metro Manila — Styrofoam fibers whizz out of a battered refrigerator as Joanna Amican, a 46-year-old waste picker in Malabon, hammers the steel walls and insulation of the appliance to get to the metal pipes to sell later.

She inhales the fibers, far too small to be visible to the naked eye. Other waste pickers breathe in metallic dust or cut themselves on open wounds while dismantling electronic waste with their bare hands. They have done this for decades to sell recycled precious metals, make ends meet, and put food on the table.
Some of these communities are adjacent to landfills, where they source broken appliances directly.

But government authorities have long persecuted the informal recycling community. Without access to formal recycling programs, police see waste pickers as regular Clean Air Act violators. When Amican and her waste pickers were just starting out, police regularly apprehended them for dismantling refrigerators and air conditioners out in the open.

Image: A wasteworker recovers the copper piping off a heat exchanger. Using only a cutter, he separates the metallic fins from the copper pipes, sending metallic dust into his face. (Alex Lauricio/Philippine Collegian)

A wasteworker recovers the copper piping off a heat exchanger. Using only a cutter, he separates the metallic fins from the copper pipes, sending metallic dust into his face. (Alex Lauricio/Philippine Collegian)

“Hinuhuli kami dahil sa illegal na pagbabaklas kung saan-saan, na ayon sa batas RA 6969, yung Clean Air Act, hindi dapat tayo nagpapausok o nagpapalabas ng hazard o toxic waste sa lansangan,” said Amican. Certain components of these appliances contain freon gas made of ozone-destroying chlorofluorocarbons.

Despite being part and parcel of the domestic recycling sector, government subsidies for advanced recycling technologies are nonexistent. This infrastructure—necessary to safely dismantle air conditioning units and other appliances with freon gas—can help waste workers reduce the amount of electronic waste that ends up in landfills.

### Alex Lauricio

Junk shop hotspots in Malabon, Montalban, and Payatas recycle precious metals from landfills back to industries, but face health risks from increasingly toxic waste shipments from the Global North.

As hazardous waste funneled from foreign countries piles up in the Philippines, informal waste workers struggle to survive while cleaning up after a system that leaves them behind. (Design by Angelique Cochingyan)

Styrofoam fibers whizz out of a battered refrigerator as Joanna Amican, a 46-year-old scavenger in Malabon, hammers the steel walls and insulation of the appliance to get to the metal pipes to sell later.

She inhales the fibers, far too small to be visible to the naked eye. Health and other safety hazards, including microplastic dust, endanger waste workers who work with discarded plastic bottles from landfills, or with unrepatriated waste illegally dumped by wealthier nations in the Philippines.

Poor safety conditions and management results in unnecessary risks for wasteworkers and residents living near landfills.

Unconsultative and poorly planned adoption of WtE technologies is not a solution for decades-long dependence on landfills. Pushing back starts by scaling waste management down to smaller, community-controlled facilities within each LGU, stripping corporations of mega-profits amidst the growing waste management market.

Such attempts at community waste management include the recent efforts of Siquijor to be recognized as the first Zero Waste island, categorized by the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives, a global network supporting climate action by communities. Siquijor’s intuitive approach and investment in its 89 community-run material recovery facilities across its barangays took away volumes of trash from its mountains and beaches, and the need for corporate-funded technologies.

While it can be argued that the island is small, its developed waste management could be expanded in places with bigger regional landfills, easing the disproportionate waste burden that major cities currently force upon a handful of communities.

More than Siquijor’s success in implementing the Zero Waste agenda, each community’s responsibility to their own waste translates to consciousness about what they produce and consume. In this way, communities can finally push back against the private waste market and treat sanitation as a social right more than a business venture.

Vulnerable communities must resist the continued construction of landfill facilities while also being active participants of the Zero Waste agenda. Their safety must be guaranteed so that no technology will ever bury another wasteworker for the sake of profit. If the state cannot stomach the visceral image of garbage outside its halls of power, no house bill or corporate partnership will save it from the impending collapse. ◆

First published in the June 18, 2026 print edition of the Collegian.
